passage: In the kasba school near Rampur, the maths period began, and Hafsa's palms went damp. Avni Didi drew a clock and asked, "How many minutes till twelve?" The hands looked like they were sliding. Hafsa stared at her slate and said nothing, her ears burning. Yet that same morning she had written a poem about the monsoon that Avni Didi read aloud twice. After class, Avni Didi brought out a jar of tamarind seeds and a paper clock with a moving hand. "Tomorrow and every day, ten minutes, just us." She never said "careless." By the end of the month Hafsa could count out thirty seeds in fives and move the paper hand to half past.

qa.q: What did Avni Didi bring out after class?
qa.a: She brought out a jar of tamarind seeds and a paper clock with a moving hand.

qa.q: How did Hafsa feel when asked about the minutes till twelve?
qa.a: She felt panicked and embarrassed; her palms were damp, her ears burned and she could not answer.

qa.q: Why did Avni Didi's approach work?
qa.a: She used hands-on seeds and a paper clock, repeated it patiently every day and never called Hafsa careless, so Hafsa could make progress.

qa.q: How might Avni Didi see Hafsa, given the monsoon poem?
qa.a: Avni Didi sees a gifted writer who struggles with numbers, not a lazy or dull student.

grounding: Shows a child who panics over time and quantity despite a gift for language, making progress through hands-on materials and patient, shame-free repetition.

passage: In Cebu, Paulo, nine, missed the school bus again because he could not tell when "a quarter to" was. In the maths quiz the next morning, the numbers blurred and his chest went tight; he drew a robot in the margin instead. His cousin Sami, home from college, found the quiz in his bag. Paulo waited for the scolding. Instead Sami cut a clock from a paper plate and strung twenty beads on a shoelace. "We'll do this every night after dinner. Slowly." Paulo's comic about the robot was taped to the fridge by then, and Sami asked him to draw the bus arriving at a quarter to.

qa.q: Why did Paulo miss the school bus?
qa.a: He could not tell when "a quarter to" was.

qa.q: What was Paulo feeling when Sami found the quiz?
qa.a: He felt scared and ashamed, waiting to be scolded for the blank maths quiz.

qa.q: What did Sami do that could help Paulo improve?
qa.a: Sami made a paper-plate clock and a bead string and planned slow practice every night, without scolding him.

qa.q: How does Sami seem to see Paulo's talents?
qa.a: Sami values Paulo's drawing and uses it, asking him to draw the bus arriving at a quarter to.

grounding: Shows a child who struggles with time and quantity and freezes in maths but is gifted at art, helped by hands-on tools and patient, unshaming practice.

passage: In the school's resource room, Ojas, eleven, wrote "21" when Asif Sir had said "twelve," then rubbed it out so hard the page tore. "I'm useless at this," he muttered. In English class he had just won the story prize, but numbers never stayed where he put them. Asif Sir did not sigh. He tipped a box of wooden blocks onto the table. "Build twelve for me. One ten-rod, two little cubes." Ojas built it. Then twenty-one. He looked at both side by side for a long time. "They're not the same at all," he said slowly. They built numbers again the next day, and the next.

qa.q: What did Ojas write when Asif Sir said "twelve"?
qa.a: He wrote "21" and then rubbed it out so hard the page tore.

qa.q: What does Ojas rubbing the page so hard suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he felt frustrated and ashamed, calling himself useless even though he is good at writing stories.

qa.q: Which part of Asif Sir's response helped most?
qa.a: He did not sigh or shame Ojas; he used wooden blocks so Ojas could see and build the difference, and repeated it each day.

qa.q: How might Asif Sir see Ojas as a learner?
qa.a: Asif Sir likely sees a capable boy who needs to handle numbers with his hands, not someone who is useless.

grounding: Shows a child who struggles to grasp quantity despite strength in language, progressing with hands-on materials and patient repetition.

passage:
Thursday night.
Saurabh's report card came today. Maths: 34. I am his mother, and I sat on the bed and felt sick. At the lift, Mrs Bhatia said her son "just does tuition, simple." I smiled and wanted to scream.
Part of me wants to sit with him for two hours every night and drill tables. Part of me wants to hide the report and tell him marks don't matter. Neither feels right.
I met his class teacher after school. She said he tries hard and suggested the school's learning support twice a week. We agreed to try.
Then Saurabh showed me the clay temple he made for art. Every tiny bell. I put it on the TV shelf where everyone will see it.

qa.q: What mark did Saurabh get in maths?
qa.a: He got 34 in maths.

qa.q: How did the mother feel about pushing or protecting Saurabh?
qa.a: She felt torn and anxious, wanting both to drill him every night and to hide the report and tell him marks don't matter.

qa.q: What steps help keep the family steady?
qa.a: Meeting the class teacher, agreeing to try learning support and proudly displaying Saurabh's clay temple to celebrate his talent.

qa.q: How might Saurabh feel seeing the clay temple on the TV shelf?
qa.a: Saurabh may feel proud and valued, knowing his mother celebrates what he is good at, not only his maths marks.

grounding: Shows a parent worried about grades and others' comments, torn between pushing and protecting, who works with the school and celebrates her child's other talent.

passage: At the family lunch in Udvada, Zubin's aunt looked at Reena's notebook and clicked her tongue. "Nine years old and still can't do sums? In our day we got a slap." Reena slid under the table with her plate. Zubin felt his face heat. That night, closing the bakery, he wondered whether he should make her do extra sums before bed, or just let her be. In the morning he walked to the school and sat with her teacher, who showed him how Reena counted on her fingers under the desk. They made a plan: counters at home, no timed tests for now. On the way back Reena sang the whole bakery jingle she had made up, and Zubin sang it with her.

qa.q: Where did Zubin sit with Reena's teacher?
qa.a: He walked to the school in the morning and sat with her teacher there.

qa.q: How did Zubin feel after his aunt's comment?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and torn, his face heating, unsure whether to push Reena with extra sums or just let her be.

qa.q: What did Zubin do that was wise?
qa.a: He worked with the teacher on a clear plan, counters at home and no timed tests for now, instead of reacting to his aunt.

qa.q: What was the family lunch like for Reena?
qa.a: It was probably humiliating and frightening, which is why she slid under the table with her plate.

grounding: Shows a parent hurt by a relative's comment and torn between pushing and protecting, who works with the school and enjoys his child's other talents.

passage: In Berlin, Selin read the class chat on her phone: another parent had posted the maths results, "Proud of our girl, top again!" Selin put the phone face down. Ines, eight, had cried over her number homework for an hour. Selin wanted to hire a tutor for every afternoon; she also wanted to write to the school and say, "Leave her alone." Instead she asked for a meeting. The teacher suggested blocks at home and extra help on Wednesdays, and told her Ines explained football tactics better than anyone. That weekend Selin stood by the pitch and cheered every pass Ines made. At home, the maths blocks sat on the kitchen table, ready for ten minutes a day.

qa.q: How long had Ines cried over her number homework?
qa.a: She had cried over her number homework for an hour.

qa.q: How did Selin feel reading the other parent's post?
qa.a: She felt hurt and anxious, putting the phone face down while comparing it with Ines's struggle.

qa.q: Which choice helped Selin more than hiring a daily tutor or confronting the school?
qa.a: Asking for a meeting and working with the teacher on blocks at home and extra help on Wednesdays.

qa.q: How might Ines experience her mother cheering at the pitch?
qa.a: Ines may feel confident and loved, seeing that her mother is proud of her football even when maths is hard.

grounding: Shows a parent worried by grades and comparisons, torn between pushing and protecting, who works with the school and celebrates her child's talent.

passage:
Note from Manjula, English teacher, Class 10.
Lalit tells the best stories in the class. When we read the chapter on the flood, he retold it with such detail that two students gasped. His notebooks are full of diagrams and little drawings of every scene. But in timed tests he writes half a page, the spellings scrambled, and hands in the paper with his head down. Last week he said, "I know it, ma'am. I just can't get it out fast enough."
I spoke to his parents that afternoon and suggested an assessment. The report came yesterday. With the board's permission, he will now get extra time and a reader in exams. In Friday's practice test with extra time, he scored his highest mark this year.

qa.q: What did Lalit's notebooks contain?
qa.a: They are full of diagrams and little drawings of every scene.

qa.q: How does Lalit feel when handing in timed tests?
qa.a: He feels discouraged and ashamed, handing in the paper with his head down because he cannot write what he knows fast enough.

qa.q: Why was suggesting an assessment the right step?
qa.a: It showed the real difficulty and led to permitted extra time and a reader, so his marks could reflect what he actually knows.

qa.q: How might Lalit's parents feel about the practice test result?
qa.a: They are likely relieved and proud, seeing clear proof that Lalit knows the work when given fair conditions.

grounding: Shows a teenager who thinks in pictures and tells stories brilliantly but struggles with spelling and speed under time limits, helped by assessment and accommodations.

passage:
Monday.
Prelims history paper today. I KNEW the answers. I could see the whole battle like a film in my head: the river, the horses, who moved first. But three hours wasn't enough. I wrote slow, crossed out spellings, and the bell rang with two questions blank. Baljeet asked how it went and I said "fine" and walked off.
Then this evening Mummy and I went to the clinic for the assessment the school counsellor suggested. The psychologist had me read, spell, do puzzles. At the end she said I reason really well, and that I can apply for extra time in the boards.
I don't feel stupid tonight. For the first time I feel like the marks might finally match my head.
Vaibhav

qa.q: How many questions did Vaibhav leave blank?
qa.a: Vaibhav left two questions blank when the bell rang.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav feel when Baljeet asked about the paper?
qa.a: Vaibhav felt frustrated and embarrassed, saying "fine" and walking off because the answers were known but not written in time.

qa.q: What step made the difference for Vaibhav?
qa.a: Going for the assessment the counsellor suggested, which showed strong reasoning and opened the way to apply for extra time in the boards.

qa.q: What might Baljeet think when Vaibhav walks off after saying "fine"?
qa.a: Baljeet might feel confused or brushed off, not knowing how upset Vaibhav really was about the paper.

grounding: Shows a teenager who sees history like a film but struggles with spelling and speed under time limits, and gets an assessment leading to permitted extra time.

subtype: Teacher noticing a gap between effort and results [Observer]
passage:
Teacher's note, Ganga, History, Class 9.
In Tuesday's discussion on the salt march, Nitin spoke for five minutes without notes, linking the march to prices in his own grandfather's village. It was the best answer anyone gave. Then I marked his written test: four lines per answer, many words misspelt, one answer left unfinished. He had clearly tried; there were rubbings-out all over. The mismatch was too big to be laziness.
I stopped calling on him to read the textbook aloud without warning; he now gets the passage a day earlier. I phoned his parents that evening and suggested a screening with the school counsellor. In my marking I now give separate credit for ideas. Next step: meet the counsellor on Monday.

qa.q: What topic did Nitin speak about for five minutes?
qa.a: He spoke about the salt march, linking it to prices in his grandfather's village.

qa.q: How did Ganga feel on seeing the gap between Nitin's discussion and written test?
qa.a: Ganga felt puzzled and concerned, sensing the mismatch was too big to be laziness.

qa.q: What did Ganga do that separated a learning difference from lack of effort?
qa.a: Ganga stopped surprise reading aloud, gave the passage early, suggested screening to his parents and gave separate credit for ideas.

qa.q: How might Nitin feel about getting the passage a day early?
qa.a: Nitin may feel relieved and less anxious, able to prepare instead of fearing being put on the spot.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing strong oral answers but weak written work, and responding with screening, no surprise reading aloud and credit for ideas.

passage:
Wednesday night, staff room diary.
Avni, Class 11, stays after every physics class to redo problems. Her working is careful and neat, but the final numbers keep going wrong: 36 becomes 63, a minus sign vanishes. Today a boy said, "She just doesn't try," and she went red. It isn't true. I've watched her try harder than anyone.
When she brought me her notebook, the students were still calling me "Ujjwal Sir" through the doorway, and I kept my voice low. I said, "Your method is right. Let's look at the numbers together." I will not ask her to solve at the board in front of everyone again. Tomorrow I'll speak to her parents about screening for a number difficulty, and I'll mark her method separately.

qa.q: What happens to 36 in Avni's working?
qa.a: 36 becomes 63.

qa.q: How did Ujjwal Sir feel when the boy said Avni doesn't try?
qa.a: He felt protective and frustrated, knowing he had watched her try harder than anyone.

qa.q: Which of Ujjwal Sir's plans treats this as a learning difference rather than laziness?
qa.a: Suggesting screening for a number difficulty to her parents, marking her method separately and not putting her on the spot at the board.

qa.q: How might Avni have felt when the boy made his comment?
qa.a: Avni probably felt humiliated and hurt, going red because her real effort was being called laziness.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing careful effort with repeated number errors, and responding with screening, no on-the-spot tasks and credit for method.

passage:
Tuesday
Today I finally did it. I went to Professor Joseph's office after the lecture and told him I have dyslexia and need extra time in the mid-sems. My voice shook. I had rehearsed it on the bus while my audiobook played, but I still stared at his bookshelf the whole time.
He just nodded. "Thanks for telling me, Payal. Send me the certificate and I'll arrange it. And your essay on migration was excellent." EXCELLENT.
I walked out grinning like an idiot. All through school I hid it. Now I use my voice-typing app for notes, audiobooks for readings, and I'm not ashamed of any of it. My brain works. It just takes a different road.

qa.q: What does Payal use for notes and readings now?
qa.a: Payal uses a voice-typing app for notes and audiobooks for readings.

qa.q: How did Payal feel while telling Professor Joseph?
qa.a: Payal felt very nervous and embarrassed, voice shaking and eyes fixed on his bookshelf.

qa.q: What made asking for extra time worth it?
qa.a: Professor Joseph agreed straight away and praised Payal's essay, which showed that sharing the difference led to understanding.

qa.q: How might Professor Joseph see Payal after the conversation?
qa.a: He likely sees Payal as a capable student with an excellent essay, whose request is simple to arrange.

grounding: Shows a young adult who uses audiobooks, voice tools and extra time, feels embarrassed to ask at first, and finds that sharing earns understanding and pride.

passage: At the agricultural training centre in a small town near Thrissur, Shankar, twenty, had avoided writing the soil report for a week. Words slipped around on the page. His classmates typed fast. That evening, under the tamarind tree, he spoke his whole report into a voice-to-text tool on his phone, sentence by sentence, about the red soil, the paddy, the drainage. Next morning he knocked on Jomon Sir's door, his heart thumping. "Sir, I have a reading difficulty. I did it by voice. Is that allowed?" Jomon read it twice. "Allowed? This is the best drainage plan in the batch." Shankar walked back to the fields with his shoulders straight.

grounding: Shows a young adult using a voice tool, feeling embarrassed to ask, and finding that sharing his difference earns understanding and shows real ability.

passage: The village school near Kottayam had no electric bell; the peon struck an iron plate with a rod. Every time, Joseph, nine, dived under his desk. The older boys called him a coward, and one teacher called it drama. Aparna Teacher watched for a week. Then she moved his seat to the far end of the verandah, away from the plate, and let him cover his ears with a folded scarf. On Friday she asked, "Would you like to strike the bell at the last period?" Joseph held the rod, knowing exactly when the sound would come. He struck it three times and grinned.

qa.q: How was the bell rung at the village school?
qa.a: The peon struck an iron plate with a rod.

qa.q: How did Joseph feel each time the bell rang?
qa.a: He felt frightened and overwhelmed by the sudden loud sound, diving under his desk.

qa.q: What did Aparna Teacher do that was wiser than calling it drama?
qa.a: She observed him, moved his seat away from the plate, let him cover his ears and gave him control of the bell.

passage: In the changing room at the sports club, Farhan, eight, flung the new team jersey on the bench. "It's scratchy! It's burning me!" His mother, Zeenat, sighed loudly. "You are being fussy. passage: "Harsha, you think your Nani was always this calm about clothes? When I was eight, my mother bought me a woollen frock for Diwali. The wool scratched like ants all over my skin. I cried and tore at it, and she said, 'Such drama! Other girls are happy with new clothes.' I felt so ashamed. Then my own Nani came to visit. She saw my arms, all red. She didn't argue with my mother. She just said, 'Let the child tell us.' I told her. That winter she knitted a jumper from soft cotton yarn and sewed a cotton lining into the frock. From then on, my mother always let me feel the cloth first. No more fights. That is why I always ask you before I buy you anything."

qa.q: What did Nani's own Nani knit for her?
qa.a: She knitted her a jumper from soft cotton yarn and sewed a cotton lining into the frock.

qa.q: How did the young girl in the story feel when her mother called it drama?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and misunderstood, because the wool really scratched her skin like ants.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story?
qa.a: Her Nani saw her red arms and said to let the child tell them, then believed her and made cotton clothes, which ended the fights.

qa.q: How might the girl's mother have seen things differently after the cotton lining?
qa.a: The mother likely realised the discomfort was real, not drama, and began letting her daughter feel the cloth first.

grounding: An elder recalls being seen as dramatic about scratchy clothes until a relative listened, believed her and made small changes that ended the battles.

passage: I'm Suraj, and at sixteen I thought I was just a restless kid. I bounced my knee in every class, chewed my hoodie strings, needed to slam a football against the wall before I could study. Teachers told me to sit still. My friend Bidisha was the opposite. She hated the canteen noise, wouldn't eat anything slimy, and covered her ears at assemblies. We used to joke we were two broken radios. Then in Class 11 our biology teacher explained that some bodies seek more input and some avoid it. That made sense to me. I started doing push-ups before exams and keeping a stress ball in my pocket. Bidisha started eating lunch in the courtyard. We weren't broken. We were just learning how to tune ourselves.

qa.q: What did Suraj need to do before studying?
qa.a: Suraj needed to slam a football against the wall.

qa.q: How did Suraj feel about the restlessness before Class 11?
qa.a: Suraj felt misunderstood and a bit ashamed, being told to sit still and joking about being a broken radio.

qa.q: How did self-knowledge change things for Suraj?
qa.a: Understanding the need for input led Suraj to plan push-ups before exams and carry a stress ball.

qa.q: How might Bidisha feel after starting to eat in the courtyard?
qa.a: Bidisha may feel calmer and more comfortable, away from the canteen noise that bothered her.

grounding: Shows one teenager who seeks input by moving and chewing and another who avoids noise and textures, both learning to plan with self-knowledge.
